body:
Locating places on the Earth

The Earth is approximately spherical, although it is slightly flattened at the poles and bulges around the Equator. To identify the exact location of a place on its curved surface, geographers use a system of imaginary reference lines known as the geographical grid or graticule.

This grid consists of 2 sets of lines: parallels of latitude and meridians of longitude. Together, they provide the geographical coordinates of a place.

Earth's axis and poles

The Earth rotates around an imaginary line called its axis. The 2 points at which this axis meets the Earth's surface are the North Pole and the South Pole. These poles provide natural reference points for establishing the geographical grid.

Latitude

Latitude is the angular position of a place north or south of the Equator, expressed in degrees.

The Equator is an imaginary circle located midway between the North Pole and the South Pole. It has a latitude of 0° and divides the Earth into the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.

Lines joining places with the same latitude are called parallels of latitude. They run in an east-west direction and remain parallel to the Equator.

  • Latitude increases from 0° at the Equator to 90° at either pole.
  • North Pole: 90°N.
  • South Pole: 90°S.
  • The Equator is the longest parallel of latitude.
  • The circumference of each parallel decreases towards the poles.
  • The poles themselves are points rather than circles.

Longitude

Longitude is the angular position of a place east or west of the Prime Meridian, expressed in degrees.

Lines joining places with the same longitude are called meridians of longitude. Each meridian extends from the North Pole to the South Pole.

The reference meridian for measuring longitude is the Prime Meridian, assigned the value of 0°. The International Meridian Conference held in Washington, D.C., in 1884 selected the Greenwich meridian as the common international reference.

Greenwich is situated in London, United Kingdom, and is associated with the Royal Observatory.

  • Longitudes extend from 0° to 180°E and from 0° to 180°W.
  • 180°E and 180°W represent the same meridian.
  • The Prime Meridian and the 180° meridian together divide the Earth into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres.
  • All meridians have equal lengths and meet at both poles.
  • The distance between neighbouring meridians is greatest at the Equator and decreases towards the poles.

Expressing geographical coordinates

Latitude and longitude are angular measurements. Each degree is divided into 60 minutes of arc, and each minute of arc is divided into 60 seconds of arc.

  • 1° = 60′.
  • 1′ = 60″.
  • 1° = 3,600″.
  • 23.5° is equivalent to 23°30′.

The conventional order for writing geographical coordinates is latitude followed by longitude. For example, a place at 23°N, 72°E is located 23° north of the Equator and 72° east of the Prime Meridian. Its position is determined by the intersection of these 2 lines.

Latitude alone cannot normally identify a unique place because many places lie along the same parallel. Similarly, a longitude passes through many places between the poles.

Parallels run east-west but measure position north or south. Meridians run north-south but measure position east or west.

Prelims focus

  • Equator: 0° latitude.
  • Prime Meridian: 0° longitude.
  • Latitude ranges from 0° to 90° in either hemisphere.
  • Longitude ranges from 0° to 180° east or west.
  • The Greenwich meridian was internationally selected in 1884.
  • Trap: 180°E and 180°W are not separate meridians.

[References: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 10–13; NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Class 11, Chapter 3, pp. 26–29; Royal Museums Greenwich, Stand on the Prime Meridian Greenwich, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Latitude, Longitude and the Geographical Grid

body:
Geometrical differences

Parallels of latitude and meridians of longitude serve different geographical purposes. Their shapes, lengths and spacing follow from the approximately spherical form of the Earth.

FeatureParallels of latitudeMeridians of longitude
Reference lineEquatorPrime Meridian
DirectionEast-westNorth-south
ShapeCircles, except the polesSemicircles
LengthDecreases towards polesEqual
RelationshipRemain parallelMeet at both poles
Major applicationHeat zones and north-south positionLocal time and east-west position

Meridians intersect the Equator and other parallels at right angles on a globe.

Number of parallels and meridians

Geographical coordinates can be expressed to any required degree of precision. Therefore, there is no fixed limit to the number of possible parallels and meridians. However, school geography commonly counts them at intervals of 1°.

Latitude at 1° intervals

  • 89 circular parallels north of the Equator, from 1°N to 89°N.
  • 89 circular parallels south of the Equator, from 1°S to 89°S.
  • 1 Equator.
  • 2 poles, at 90°N and 90°S.

There are therefore 179 circular parallels at 1° intervals, or 181 distinct integer latitude values when the 2 poles are included.

Longitude at 1° intervals

There are 179 meridians from 1°E to 179°E, another 179 from 1°W to 179°W, and the 0° and 180° meridians. This produces 360 distinct meridians at intervals of 1°.

Distance between geographical coordinates

A difference of 1° of latitude represents approximately 111 km along a meridian. The distance is nearly constant because latitudes are measured along north-south arcs of the Earth. The Earth's slight flattening causes small variations in this value.

A difference of 1° of longitude, however, does not represent a constant ground distance. The same angular separation corresponds to a progressively shorter distance as latitude increases.

  • At the Equator, 1° of longitude represents approximately 111 km.
  • At latitude 60°, it represents approximately 56 km.
  • At either pole, the separation between meridians becomes zero.

This explains why a country extending across nearly 30° of latitude and 30° of longitude need not have equal north-south and east-west dimensions.

Great circles and small circles

In the spherical model of the Earth, a great circle divides the globe into 2 equal hemispheres. Its plane passes through the centre of the Earth. The shorter great-circle arc between 2 non-antipodal points represents the shortest surface route on a sphere.

A small circle does not divide the globe into equal hemispheres.

  • The Equator is the only parallel of latitude that is a great circle.
  • All other circular parallels are small circles.
  • A meridian is a semicircle. A meridian together with its opposite meridian forms a great circle.

For example, the 0° and 180° meridians form a great circle, as do the 30°E and 150°W meridians.

Antipodes

Two places situated at diametrically opposite positions on the Earth are called antipodes. In the spherical model, a straight line joining them through the Earth passes through its centre.

To determine the antipode of an ordinary geographical coordinate:

  1. Retain the numerical value of the latitude but reverse north and south.
  2. Subtract the longitude from 180° and reverse east and west.

The antipode of 20°N, 70°E is 20°S, 110°W. The latitude changes hemisphere, while the opposite longitude is 180° − 70° = 110°.

A point on the Equator has its antipode on the Equator. The North Pole and South Pole are antipodes of each other, and longitude is not uniquely defined at either pole.

Prelims focus

  • 179 circular parallels at 1° intervals; 181 latitude values including the poles.
  • 360 distinct meridians at 1° intervals.
  • 1° of latitude represents approximately 111 km.
  • The distance between meridians decreases towards the poles.
  • The Equator is the only great circle among parallels.
  • Trap: A single meridian is a semicircle, not a complete great circle.

[References: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 11–13; NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Class 11, Chapter 3, pp. 26–30; NOAA National Ocean Service, What is latitude? and What is longitude?, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Comparing Parallels and Meridians: Distance, Direction and Antipodes

body:
The principal geographical parallels

Certain parallels of latitude have special geographical significance because they mark the boundaries of major zones of solar heating and seasonal daylight.

Their positions are related to the inclination of the Earth's axis. The axis is inclined approximately 23.5° from the perpendicular to the plane of its orbit around the Sun, or 66.5° to the orbital plane itself.

The conventional rounded values used in school geography are:

  • North Pole: 90°N.
  • Arctic Circle: 66°30′N.
  • Tropic of Cancer: 23°30′N.
  • Equator: 0°.
  • Tropic of Capricorn: 23°30′S.
  • Antarctic Circle: 66°30′S.
  • South Pole: 90°S.

The actual astronomical positions of the tropics and polar circles vary slightly over long periods because the Earth's axial inclination changes. The rounded values above are the standard values for elementary geographical calculations.

Why the Earth is heated unequally

The amount of incoming solar energy received by a unit area of the Earth's surface depends partly on the angle at which the Sun's rays strike it.

When solar rays arrive nearly vertically, their energy is concentrated over a relatively small area. When they arrive obliquely, the same quantity of energy spreads over a larger surface. Oblique rays also travel through a greater depth of the atmosphere.

Consequently, low latitudes generally receive more intense solar radiation than high latitudes. This relationship provides the basis for dividing the Earth into broad astronomical heat zones.

The 3 types of heat zones

Torrid Zone

The Torrid Zone, also called the tropical zone, extends from the Tropic of Cancer at 23°30′N to the Tropic of Capricorn at 23°30′S.

It is the only geographical zone in which the Sun can be directly overhead at local solar noon. Places strictly between the tropics normally experience the overhead Sun twice a year, while the tropics themselves experience it once a year, in the ideal astronomical model.

The total latitudinal extent of the Torrid Zone is approximately 47°.

Temperate Zones

There are 2 Temperate Zones:

  • North Temperate Zone: Between the Tropic of Cancer and the Arctic Circle, from 23°30′N to 66°30′N.
  • South Temperate Zone: Between the Tropic of Capricorn and the Antarctic Circle, from 23°30′S to 66°30′S.

Each Temperate Zone has a latitudinal extent of approximately 43°. At locations strictly within these zones, the Sun is never directly overhead. Its altitude and the duration of daylight vary considerably with the seasons.

Frigid Zones

The Frigid Zones, also called polar zones, extend from the polar circles to their respective poles.

  • North Frigid Zone: From 66°30′N to 90°N.
  • South Frigid Zone: From 66°30′S to 90°S.

Each Frigid Zone has a latitudinal extent of approximately 23.5°. Solar rays generally strike these regions at low angles, and there are extreme seasonal variations in the duration of daylight.

There are 3 types of heat zones but 5 geographical heat belts: 1 Torrid Zone, 2 Temperate Zones and 2 Frigid Zones.

The relationship between the tropics and polar circles

The tropics mark the northernmost and southernmost latitudes at which the Sun can appear directly overhead. The polar circles mark the approximate limits beyond which continuous daylight or continuous darkness for at least 24 hours is possible during part of the year.

The poles experience approximately 6 months of daylight and 6 months of darkness in the simplified astronomical model. Locations closer to the polar circles experience much shorter periods of continuous daylight and darkness.

Heat zones are not exact climate boundaries

The broad heat zones describe astronomical conditions rather than the actual temperature of every location. Altitude, ocean currents, distance from the sea and cloud cover also influence temperature.

For example, a high mountain in the Torrid Zone can be much colder than a low-lying area at a higher latitude. This does not change the mountain's geographical heat zone.

Prelims focus

  • Tropics: approximately 23°30′ north and south.
  • Polar circles: approximately 66°30′ north and south.
  • The Torrid Zone extends across approximately 47° of latitude.
  • Each Temperate Zone extends across approximately 43°.
  • Direct overhead sunlight occurs only within the tropics, including their boundaries.
  • Trap: All places in the Frigid Zones do not experience 6 months of continuous daylight.

[References: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018–19 reprint, Chapters 2–3, pp. 11–12 and 18–21; NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Class 11, Chapter 3, p. 30; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Chapter 9, Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature.]

title: Important Latitudes and the Heat Zones of the Earth

body:
Movement of the overhead Sun

As the Earth revolves around the Sun, its inclined axis maintains approximately the same orientation in space. This causes the latitude receiving the Sun's vertical rays to shift northward and southward during the year.

The latitude at which the Sun is directly overhead at local solar noon is called the subsolar latitude. Its annual movement is restricted to the region between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.

The subsolar latitude never moves north of approximately 23°30′N or south of approximately 23°30′S. These limits explain the geographical significance of the 2 tropics.

Equinoxes

During an equinox, neither hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun more than the other. The vertical rays of the Sun fall on the Equator, and day and night are approximately equal in duration across most of the world.

There are 2 equinoxes each year, occurring around 20–21 March and 22–23 September. Elementary textbooks commonly represent them using 21 March and 23 September.

The Equator experiences the directly overhead Sun on both equinoxes.

Solstices

June solstice

Around 21 June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun. The vertical rays reach the Tropic of Cancer, approximately 23°30′N. This is the northern limit of the Sun's annual overhead position.

The Northern Hemisphere experiences summer conditions, while the Southern Hemisphere experiences winter conditions. Within the Arctic Circle, continuous daylight occurs for varying periods depending on latitude.

December solstice

Around 21–22 December, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun. The vertical rays reach the Tropic of Capricorn, approximately 23°30′S.

The Southern Hemisphere experiences summer conditions, while the Northern Hemisphere experiences winter conditions. The Antarctic polar region receives continuous daylight for varying periods, whereas the Arctic polar region experiences corresponding periods of darkness.

The exact calendar date and time of a solstice or equinox vary slightly from year to year.

Latitude and duration of daylight

Latitude affects not only the angle of incoming sunlight but also the seasonal variation in the length of the day.

  • Near the Equator, daylight and darkness remain approximately 12 hours each throughout the year.
  • Seasonal differences in day length generally become greater towards the poles.
  • Near the Arctic and Antarctic Circles, the difference between summer and winter daylight becomes extreme.
  • At the poles, the ideal astronomical model gives approximately half a year of daylight followed by half a year of darkness.

The polar circles are therefore significant as daylight boundaries, whereas the tropics are significant as overhead-Sun boundaries.

Application to Gujarat

The Tropic of Cancer passes through Gujarat. Locations in Gujarat south of this parallel lie within the Torrid Zone and can experience the Sun directly overhead at solar noon. Locations north of it lie outside the astronomical tropics and cannot experience a directly overhead Sun.

The Tropic of Cancer itself marks the northernmost limit at which this phenomenon occurs, around the June solstice.

A directly overhead Sun is not the same as a Sun that appears high in the sky. A place north of the Tropic of Cancer may experience very hot summer conditions even though the Sun never reaches its exact zenith there.

Prelims focus

  • March and September equinoxes: overhead Sun at the Equator.
  • June solstice: overhead Sun at the Tropic of Cancer.
  • December solstice: overhead Sun at the Tropic of Capricorn.
  • The seasonal variation in daylight generally increases with latitude.
  • The Tropic of Cancer passes through Gujarat.
  • Trap: A solstice in one hemisphere does not produce the same season in the opposite hemisphere.

[References: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 3, pp. 18–21; Department of Education, Government of NCT of Delhi, Class 10 Social Science Support Material, NIOS Project, 2025, p. 45, consulted 26 November 2026.]
